t: LeetCode 2135 - Count Words Obtained After Adding a Letter: Letter Sets as Bitmasks
o: **Understanding the problem.** From a start word you must append one brand-new letter (one not already present), then may rearrange letters freely; so a target is reachable iff its set of letters equals some start word's letter set plus exactly one fresh letter. In example 1, "tack" comes from "act" plus 'k' and "acti" from "act" plus 'i', but "act" itself matches nothing because the append step is mandatory even though "act" sits in startWords - giving 2. In example 2 only "abc" is reachable (from "ab" + 'c'); "abcd" would need source "abc", which is absent, so the answer is 1. Crucially no word repeats a letter, so each word is fully described by its SET of letters, and lengths up to 26 invite 26-bit integer masks.
k: Append-new-letter plus free rearrangement means target and source share letter sets except for one extra target letter.
Because no word repeats a letter, a 26-bit mask captures a word completely.
A target counts iff clearing exactly one of its mask bits lands in the set of start masks.

a.i: Canonicalize every start word by sorting its letters and store the result in a hash set. Sorting neutralizes the rearrangement step; trying every single-character deletion of the sorted target covers all possible source words. The first successful lookup counts that target. This version needs no bit tricks and generalizes naturally to alphabets with repeats handled differently.
s: Store ''.join(sorted(w)) for every start word in a hash set.
For each target word, build its sorted form s.
For each index i, check whether s with character i removed exists in the set.
Count the target if any deletion matches.
a.t: O((S+T) * L log L) for S starts, T targets, length L <= 26 - sorting canonical forms dominates
a.sp: O(S * L) - stored canonical start words

a.i: Map each word to mask = OR of (1 << (letter - 'a')); since letters never repeat, this loses nothing. A target's mask with one set bit cleared must land in the set of start masks - that cleared bit is precisely the appended letter. Probing at most 26 candidate clears replaces string surgery with cheap integer operations.
s: Build the set of masks for all start words.
For each target, compute its mask m.
For each bit b set in m, test whether m ^ (1 << b) is in the set.
Count the target if any probe succeeds.
a.t: O((S+T)*L + 26*T) - linear mask construction plus at most 26 probes per target
a.sp: O(S) - one integer per start word

w: Lead with the bitmask version after explaining the set-difference characterization; the sorted-deletion view justifies why ONE deletion suffices. Pitfalls: forgetting the appended letter must be ABSENT from the source (an identical word never qualifies - example 1's "act"), probing bits not present in the target, and assuming repeated letters are possible (they are guaranteed not to be, which makes masks lossless). Edge cases: length-1 targets are never obtainable, and duplicate words in targetWords count separately. Follow-ups: support insert-plus-replace transformations, or report witnessing source words via a mask-to-index map.
